title: Duty Time Versus Clock Time: A Comparative Analysis of Driver Working-Time Regulation and Time-of-Day Access Restrictions in the United States and Switzerland, with a Capacity Model for Alpine Transit Planning
content: In both the United States and Switzerland, a truck driver’s working time is now recorded electronically. Beyond that, the two systems have little in common. US federal hours-of-service (HOS) rules count time from the moment a driver comes on duty and cap how long they may drive or remain on duty. Switzerland applies driving and rest rules equivalent to those of the EU, through the Land Transport Agreement and its Chauffeur Ordinance (OTR 1). It also forbids heavy goods vehicles to drive at night (22:00-05:00) and on Sundays and public holidays, and it meters truck traffic through the Gotthard road tunnel with a dosing system. In this paper I compare the two regimes parameter by parameter as they stand in 2025–2026, including the recording devices: self-certified electronic logging devices (ELDs) in the US and type-approved smart tachographs in Switzerland. I then add a clock-time term, which has no counterpart in US federal law, to a standard remaining-capacity formula and apply it to a trip from Basel to Chiasso. Under the assumptions used, what limits the Swiss driver is not a working-time rule but the start of the night ban. A truck leaving in the late afternoon can absorb only 1.5 hours of dosing delay. Under US rules, the same trip could absorb 9.5 hours. In Switzerland, when a truck leaves matters more than how long the driver has already worked. The paper closes with propositions that can be tested against tachograph data and tunnel traffic records.
